meta.title: Who really said "Every Dogma Has Its Day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Anthony Burgess. An exact match was printed in an 1873 Washington paper, credited to an unnamed joker; Israel Zangwill used it in an 1898 speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every Dogma Has Its Day'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Anthony Burgess. The pun is Victorian: printed in 1873 with no author's name, and spoken by Israel Zangwill at a Tolstoy dinner in 1898.

answer.label: Not Anthony Burgess — an anonymous Victorian pun
answer.authorDates: First exact match in print 1 April 1873 · The Critic-Record, Washington, D.C.
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traced the wordplay to an unnamed local joker — a “merry-andrew” — whose line was reported in a Washington newspaper in 1873, and found no instance of it anywhere in Anthony Burgess’s works. The fullest documented use belongs to the novelist Israel Zangwill, who said it in a speech at a dinner for Tolstoy’s seventieth birthday, printed in The Critic in October 1898.

source.heading: The best-documented use

docMeta.dd: “Jottings About Town,” The Critic-Record (Washington, D.C.), 1 April 1873, p. 6 — credited to an unnamed local “merry-andrew” (per Quote Investigator)
“Prophetic Almanacks,” London Review, 16 December 1865, p. 639 (per Quote Investigator)
The Critic: An Illustrated Monthly Review of Literature, Art and Life, Vol. 33, no. 856, October 1898, p. 279
Israel Zangwill’s speech at the dinner for Leo Tolstoy’s seventieth birthday, Hotel St. Denis, New York, Thursday evening, 8 September 1898

source.excerpt: … because great art is greater than all dogmas, which have their short life—every dogma has its day, just as every dog has,—but great art lives on with fresh meaning and fresh inspiration every year. Therefore I regret that Tolstoy disavows his earlier work.
trail: 1865 — the half-formed version. The London Review of 16 December 1865 prints “every dog—not to say every dogma—has its day,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

1873 — the exact line, no name attached. The Washington Critic-Record of 1 April 1873 reports that decaying belief in certain articles of faith “has instigated a local merry-andrew to improve an old saying into ‘every dogma has its day’” (QI ↗; antedatings also posted to the American Dialect Society list ↗).

1898 — the first name we can put to it. Israel Zangwill speaks the exact sentence at Tolstoy’s seventieth-birthday dinner in New York; the scanned October 1898 issue of The Critic ↗ carries it on page 279.
Modern day — the name that stuck. Burgess is credited on quote sites with no source; Wikiquote’s Burgess page ↗ does not carry the line at all.
source.excerptNote: Zangwill was arguing against Tolstoy’s late repudiation of his own novels: doctrine dates, art does not.

source.rightsNote: Every documented printing of this line predates 1931: the 1873 Critic-Record report, and Zangwill’s 1898 speech as published in The Critic (copyright 1898, The Critic Co.). Both are in the public domain in the United States, and the phrase itself has no identified author to hold rights in it.

author.name: Israel Zangwill
author.kicker: Not the coiner — the earliest named voice on record
author.heading: The man with the receipt
author.bio: Israel Zangwill (21 January 1864 – 1 August 1926) was a British novelist and playwright best known for Children of the Ghetto (1892), the comic The King of Schnorrers (1894), and the play The Melting Pot (1908), which put that phrase into the American language. He was in New York in September 1898 — being heard by an American audience for the first time — when he told a room full of Tolstoy admirers that great art outlives doctrine, “every dogma has its day, just as every dog has.” He was not claiming the pun as his own: an exact match had already been printed twenty-five years earlier, credited to nobody in particular.

cite.sourceCitation: Israel Zangwill, speech at the dinner for Leo Tolstoy’s seventieth birthday, Hotel St. Denis, New York, September 8, 1898, in “In Honor of Tolstoy,” The Critic: An Illustrated Monthly Review of Literature, Art and Life 33, no. 856 (October 1898): 279. Earliest exact match documented in “Jottings About Town,” The Critic-Record (Washington, D.C.), April 1, 1873, 6, per Quote Investigator.

copyAttribution: "Every dogma has its day." — origin anonymous: an exact match was printed in The Critic-Record (Washington, D.C.) on 1 April 1873, credited to an unnamed local joker. Israel Zangwill used the line in a speech printed in The Critic, October 1898, p. 279. Commonly misattributed to Anthony Burgess, in whose works it has not been found. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Four names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is a quote with a famous owner and no author. Here is who gets credit, and what each of them actually did.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that Burgess wrote about dogmas but that the punning aphorism has not been located anywhere in the corpus of his works, and notes that BrainyQuote credits him with it. The line was in print in 1873, forty-four years before he was born.
Goodreads ↗ carries it under Burgess’s name with no book, essay or interview attached, above its own disclaimer that quotes are added by users and not verified.
Zangwill delivered the exact wording in his September 1898 Tolstoy-dinner speech, printed in The Critic that October ↗ — twenty-five years after the phrase was already in a newspaper.

In January 1898 the Des Moines Daily News credited Wells, writing in the Chap-Book, with “Every dogma must have its day” among her “Mixed Maxims,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗. That is the variant, not the line quoted today.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who made the joke: Quote Investigator concludes the evidence points to an anonymous genesis ↗, with the first exact match — in the Washington Critic-Record of 1 April 1873 — ascribed only to a local “merry-andrew.”

context.heading: Why a Victorian joke ended up with a modern novelist
lead: The pun works on a proverb that the Oxford English Dictionary traces to the 1500s — “every dog has his day” — and it needs only one letter to turn a consolation into a jab at belief. Someone worked that out in the 1860s: a London Review piece of December 1865 ↗ already had “every dog—not to say every dogma—has its day” in it, and by April 1873 a Washington paper was printing the finished form and crediting an unnamed local wit.

Lines like that travel without papers. A century later the quote databases needed a name to hang on it, and Anthony Burgess — English, bookish, quotable, dead since 1993 and therefore in no position to object — was a plausible fit. Burgess did write about dogmas. He does not appear to have written this.
detailsBody: January 1898. The Des Moines Daily News ran a column of “Mixed Maxims” including “Every dogma must have its day,” credited to the light-verse writer Carolyn Wells in the Chap-Book — a variant, not the exact line, per Quote Investigator ↗.

September 1898. About a hundred covers were laid at the Hotel St. Denis in New York on Thursday evening, 8 September, for Tolstoy’s seventieth birthday. Zangwill, on his first American platform, used the exact wording while objecting that Tolstoy had disowned his own novels. The Critic printed the speech the following month ↗.
context.pull: The line is older than the man it is credited to — by forty-four years.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states Burgess wrote about dogmas but that QI has not located this punning aphorism in the corpus of his works, that BrainyQuote credits him with it, and concludes the earliest evidence points to an anonymous genesis, with the first exact match in 1873 ascribed to an unknown 'merry-andrew'.

Quote Investigator documents the 16 December 1865 London Review 'Prophetic Almanacks' precursor (p. 639), the 1 April 1873 Critic-Record 'Jottings About Town' exact match (Washington, D.C., p. 6), Carolyn Wells's 'Every dogma must have its day' in the Des Moines Daily News of 14 January 1898 crediting the Chap-Book, and Israel Zangwill's use in The Critic, October 1898, p. 279.

The October 1898 issue of The Critic (Vol. 33, no. 856) prints Israel Zangwill's speech at the 8 September 1898 Hotel St. Denis dinner for Tolstoy's seventieth birthday, and page 279 reads 'every dogma has its day, just as every dog has,—but great art lives on with fresh meaning and fresh inspiration every year.'

The ADS-L posting lists the antedatings for the aphorism, including the 1865 London Review precursor and the 1873 Critic-Record exact match, and reports no compelling evidence that Anthony Burgess originated or popularised it.
Goodreads attributes 'Every dogma has its day.' to Anthony Burgess with no book or source cited, and displays the notice that quotes are added by the community and not verified by Goodreads.
Wikiquote's Anthony Burgess page does not contain 'Every dogma has its day' in any section, and gives his dates as 25 February 1917 – 22 November 1993.
Anthony Burgess lived 25 February 1917 – 22 November 1993 and was an English novelist, critic and composer, author of A Clockwork Orange (1962).
Israel Zangwill lived 21 January 1864 – 1 August 1926 and was a British novelist and playwright, author of Children of the Ghetto (1892), The King of Schnorrers (1894) and The Melting Pot (1908).
